title: The Houthis Enter the Iran War and Everything Gets Worse
gist: The Houthis' entry into the Iran war, triggered by a Saudi strike on a Tehran-Sanaa flight allegedly carrying IRGC personnel, has closed Saudi Arabia's Bab al-Mandab oil-export lifeline for the first time since 2022, leaving both major Gulf chokepoints under Iranian-aligned pressure and forcing Riyadh into a dilemma between escalation and a reluctant Washington.

themes.theme: Escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

insights.claim: In the week of August 9, 2026, Houthi rebels killed six people aboard a cargo ship in the Bab al-Mandab — the first fatalities since the Houthis joined the Iran war in earnest — after a month of steady escalation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Marks the first fatal Houthi attack of this new escalation phase, a concrete trigger point for shipping-insurance and Red Sea freight-risk repricing.
insights.locator: Houthi rebels reportedly killed six people aboard a cargo ship

insights.claim: The Houthis also attacked an oil refinery in the Saudi city of Jazan, targeted Saudi-backed forces in the Yemeni port city of al-Mokha (killing as many as seven), and attacked a Tanzanian-flagged ship in the Bab al-Mandab, killing six crew and rescuers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Documents direct Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure (Jazan refinery), a category of target with direct implications for Saudi oil production and export continuity.
insights.locator: A few days earlier, the Houthis attacked an oil refinery

insights.claim: Iran sent a Mahan Air flight to Sanaa on July 3 — the first direct Tehran-Sanaa flight in a decade — ostensibly to retrieve a Houthi delegation for Supreme Leader Khamenei's funeral, but according to the Saudi-supported Republic of Yemen Government it also transported IRGC personnel and materiel to Houthi-controlled Yemen, violating the UN arms embargo.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific triggering event of the current escalation chain — a covert Iran-Houthi resupply flight — which precipitated Saudi military action.
insights.locator: the Iranian regime — emboldened after withstanding over four months

insights.claim: On July 13, Saudi Arabia bombed the runways at Sanaa and Hudaydah airports to block another Tehran-Sanaa flight, but the Houthis landed anyway and retaliated by targeting Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia the same day, then announced a blockade on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea a week later and struck two oil tankers carrying Saudi crude two days after that.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Traces the specific tit-for-tat escalation sequence from airstrike to blockade to tanker attacks — the operative timeline for assessing further escalation risk.
insights.locator: On July 13, Saudi Arabia reportedly bombed the runways

insights.claim: On July 27, Saudi Arabia claimed an Iranian-supported militia in Iraq, possibly coordinating with the Houthis, targeted energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, drawing a joint response from Saudi and U.S. fighter aircraft.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Confirms direct U.S. military involvement alongside Saudi Arabia in responding to attacks on Eastern Province energy infrastructure — the heart of Saudi oil production.

themes.theme: Two Gulf chokepoints now under pressure

insights.claim: Even after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the war, Saudi Arabia had been able to export about 80 percent of its oil through the Red Sea via the Bab al-Mandab, which — combined with elevated oil prices — meant the war had had limited impact on Saudi energy revenues until the Houthis began targeting Saudi Arabia directly for the first time since 2022.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Quantifies exactly how much of Saudi oil exports (80%) depended on the Red Sea alternate route that the Houthis are now actively closing off.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia had been able to export about 80 percent of its oil through the Red Sea
insights.locator: Before the current Iran war, both the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: With the Houthis restricting navigation through the Bab al-Mandab, the United States, Saudi Arabia, and the broader global shipping community could face a situation where both major maritime chokepoints used to export the majority of the Gulf's petroleum products — Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — are simultaneously subject to manipulation by Iran and its partners.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The core risk thesis: simultaneous exposure of both Gulf oil chokepoints is a materially higher and more systemic threat to global oil-supply continuity than either alone.
insights.locator: With the Houthis restricting navigation through the Bab al-Mandab

insights.claim: The Houthis regard themselves as an independent Islamic power with their own religious legitimacy and revolutionary ideology, not merely a tool of Iran, meaning any negotiated agreement to end the broader U.S.-Iran war would almost certainly not be interpreted by the Houthis as binding on their own actions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Warns that a U.S.-Iran ceasefire alone would not stop Houthi attacks, meaning oil-market and shipping-risk premiums tied to a broader Iran deal could stay elevated even after such a deal is reached.

themes.theme: Saudi Arabia's coalition-building and the US dilemma

insights.claim: On July 30, Saudi Arabia announced the formation of a maritime coalition to defend Red Sea freedom of navigation; of 43 countries initially invited, 14 have joined so far (Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Türkiye, and Yemen), but only Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye have substantial navies, and the United States has notably not joined.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The coalition's naval capacity is concentrated in just four of 14 members, and Washington's absence signals limited near-term U.S. military commitment to defending the Red Sea route.
insights.locator: On July 30, it announced the formation of a maritime coalition

insights.claim: The May 2025 U.S.-Houthi ceasefire has held even amid the broader Iran war, and President Trump would almost certainly not want another front opened before the midterms — especially one that could push oil prices higher — while a Saudi military effort against the Houthis would nonetheless require indispensable U.S. support, creating a real dilemma for Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural conflict of interest: Trump's midterm-driven aversion to broadening the war versus Saudi Arabia's operational need for U.S. backing, a key driver of whether the conflict escalates further before U.S. midterms.
insights.locator: If Saudi Arabia feels compelled to respond to repeated Houthi attacks

insights.claim: Saudi leadership is likely to view Trump's approach through the lens of prior episodes where it felt let down by Washington: the Obama administration pressured Saudi Arabia to halt airstrikes in Yemen in 2015-16 over civilian casualties; in 2019 Trump did not respond militarily to drone strikes on Saudi Abqaiq and Khurais oil infrastructure despite saying the U.S. was 'locked and loaded'; and in 2025 the Trump administration ended a U.S. air campaign against the Houthis reportedly without advance notice to Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A three-episode track record of perceived U.S. abandonment gives Saudi Arabia strong reason to distrust U.S. follow-through, informing why Riyadh is diversifying its coalition partnerships now.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia was unenthusiastic about the Iran war from the start, hoping in principle to see the end of the Iranian regime but fearing the region would end up worse off, and expecting correctly that the U.S. would not adequately factor the kingdom's infrastructure vulnerabilities into its war planning.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames the Houthi escalation as the realization of Saudi Arabia's original worst-case fear about the Iran war, useful context for assessing how far Riyadh will go to avoid further entanglement.
insights.quote: the latest bitter fruit of this ill-conceived war the Saudi people never really wanted
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia has been unenthusiastic about the Iran war
